intro: Foundations of International Law. Unit one: the international legal order, an introduction. This is the unit that sets up everything else — what this law is, who it binds, where it comes from, and why it counts as law at all.
outro: That is the end of Unit one. The thread to hold on to: nobody stands above states, so the law that binds them is the law they consented to — and it is enforced not by a police force but by costs.

slides.3: Defining public international law. The definition sounds circular, and that is the point: this law is not identified by its subject matter but by who bears the rights and duties, and whose relations are governed. It covers relations between subjects of international law — primarily states — not between private persons. The definition closes with the words 'do not belong exclusively to the internal law of one state', and those words do the limiting work: once a matter falls entirely within a state's own domain, international law has nothing to say about it. That boundary returns later in this unit as the prohibition of intervention in internal affairs.
slides.4: What public international law is not: European Union law, and conflict of laws. These are its two closest neighbours, and the ones most often confused with it. European Union law has a cross-border dimension, but it is a supranational order sui generis: it was created by treaties between states, yet it has its own sources, its own court and direct effect on individuals, so it is not treated as ordinary international law. Conflict of law rules, that is private international law, decide which of several national laws applies to a private relationship with a foreign element — and that makes them part of domestic law, not law between states. Since the exam tests the two halves separately, this distinction also tells you which body of material a question belongs to.
slides.5: Four turning points in the history of the discipline. The course does not tell history as a story but as four moments at which the answer changed to the question of who makes the law and for whom it is valid. Classical international law, 1648 to 1918, is the law of a handful of European states that still allowed war as a lawful instrument. The October Revolution of 1917 produced a state that challenged the whole system from outside. Decolonization after 1945 multiplied the membership several times over. And the end of the East–West conflict in 1989 raised the question whether that new unity would hold — which is why the heading adds, in brackets, the word 'seeming', with a question mark. What comes now are the illustrations of those four points.
slides.6: The oldest surviving peace treaty: Kadesh. Cuneiform clay tablets in a display case at the Istanbul Archaeology Museum carry the Egyptian–Hittite peace treaty, dated to around 1280 BC. The date is not what you need to retain; the claim is. Binding agreements between powers are some three thousand years older than the modern state. The treaty as an instrument did not arrive with Westphalia; what arrived later was the system that turns a treaty into a source of law.
slides.7: 1648: the Peace of Westphalia. Gerard ter Borch painted the ratification of the Treaty of Münster — envoys around a table, hands raised in oath over the documents. Münster together with Osnabrück makes up the Peace of Westphalia, with which classical international law begins. The date has stuck for a reason: for the first time a major European settlement was negotiated by a congress of formally equal states, rather than decided by a superior authority, emperor or pope. That is the origin of the horizontal picture developed a few minutes from now.
slides.8: Grotius, and On the Law of War and Peace. Hugo Grotius is conventionally called the father of the modern discipline. He derived rules from reason and the nature of things — that is, from something that holds between rulers even where nobody stands above them. That single step, law without a superior legislator, is the foundation of the whole construction this lecture later defends against Austin's objection that international law is not law at all.
slides.9: The roots of sovereignty, first of three: par in parem non habet imperium. In the fourteenth century Bartolus de Saxoferrato formulated the maxim that an equal has no authority over an equal. It is the oldest of three quotations that together assemble the modern concept of sovereignty, and the only one with a direct procedural consequence: state immunity grows out of it, meaning the courts of one state may not sit in judgment over another.
slides.10: The roots of sovereignty, second: Bodin. In The Six Books of the Republic, 1576, Jean Bodin described sovereignty as supreme and indivisible power within the state. The quotation given here — that the rules of other states do not bind the state — is its outward-facing side. Bodin therefore answers the question of who has the last word at home. That is precisely the half which will shortly be called internal sovereignty.
slides.11: The roots of sovereignty, third: Vattel and the equality of states. In The Law of Nations, 1758, Emer de Vattel put the equality of states into an image: a dwarf is as much a man as a giant, and a small republic is no less a sovereign state than the most powerful kingdom. This is formal equality — legal status does not depend on size, population or strength. The other side of it comes soon: the equality is formal, and does not capture real differences in power.
slides.12: Solferino, 1859. Here the lecture shows Bossoli's painting of the battle with a caption and offers no explanation. In the history of the discipline, Solferino is known as the event out of which the Red Cross and the first Geneva Convention emerged — that is, the beginning of humanitarian law, which is why it usually appears in a historical overview. Check against the lecture or a textbook whether that connection was in fact drawn here; the material itself does not state it.
slides.13: CSS Alabama. The caption says only that the ship was built in Liverpool in 1862. In the history of the discipline the Alabama is associated with the Alabama claims — a dispute between the United States and Britain over breaches of the duties of a neutral state, settled by international arbitration in 1871 and 1872, and usually cited as a breakthrough in the peaceful settlement of disputes. None of that follows from the material itself, so treat it as context to verify rather than as examinable content.
slides.14: The world in 1945, shown as a map — and the colours are the argument, not decoration. Blue marks the fifty-one founding members of the United Nations. Yellow marks states outside it. The remainder, largely orange and red, are non-independent entities. What matters is what is not blue: almost all of Africa, much of South and South-East Asia, and the Caribbean. In 1945 the international community was therefore some fifty states, predominantly American and European, plus the Soviet Union and Australia. Hold that picture — what comes next is the same map eighty years later, and the difference between the two is the whole of decolonization.
slides.15: The world in 2025. The same map is now almost entirely blue: one hundred and ninety-three United Nations member states. Red marks the handful of remaining non-self-governing territories, most visibly Western Sahara and a few islands. The pair of maps is a visual argument for what the four turning points said: decolonization changed not only politics but whose consent is needed to make rules — which is why a general practice is now much harder to establish.
slides.16: International legal personality: who bears rights. Personality is not all-or-nothing; it is graded. Only states have full personality, and only states are sovereign. Partial personality belongs to intergovernmental organizations; to individuals and corporations, typically in human rights and in the criminal responsibility of individuals; and to national liberation movements and insurgents. Non-governmental organizations have none at all, however influential they are in practice — influence and legal personality are different things, and that pair is a favourite trap.
slides.17: Where personality comes from. Build the diagram in your head as a tree lying on its side. At the root stands a single box: states, original — states hold personality of their own, derived from no one. Two branches run out of it. The first branch, persons that states create, leads to international organizations. The second branch, persons that states recognize, leads to insurgents, national liberation movements, individuals, multinational corporations, the Holy See, and the International Committee of the Red Cross. The message of the whole picture is that every other personality is derived: a state either creates it or recognizes it.
slides.18: Six features of public international law — the signpost for the whole of part three. They are: state sovereignty; the territory of a state; sovereign equality; non-intervention in internal affairs; consent and sources; and state responsibility. It is worth memorising as a skeleton: in a problem question it works as a checklist of the angles from which a set of facts can be attacked.
slides.19: A horizontal legal system. Domestic law is vertical: central organs of the state make rules for all persons and objects on the territory, and enforce them from above. International law is horizontal — there is no central legislature, no court with compulsory jurisdiction, and no enforcement body. The addressees of the rules are also their authors, which is described as a system of coordination rather than subordination. This single feature explains almost everything else in the course: why the sources rest on consent, why enforcement runs through self-help, and why the question arises at all whether this is law.
slides.20: Internal and external sovereignty, set against each other. Internal sovereignty is autonomy and supreme authority to govern all people and objects on the state's own territory — and beneath it, as a newer feature, the responsibility to protect, R2P: protecting another state's population against the gravest human rights violations. External sovereignty is independence and equality of states in their mutual relations, no state subject to the authority of another, and the principle of one state, one vote in organizations and negotiations. Note where the responsibility to protect has been placed: under internal sovereignty, as a limit on it. Sovereignty no longer means that what happens inside is nobody else's business.
slides.21: Absolute versus relative sovereignty: two answers to the question whether international law binds the state at all. On the absolute view, attributed here to Hegel, international law is merely external state law, from which a state may withdraw unilaterally — in which case it is not law in any real sense. On the relative view, which prevails today, no state is subject to another state, but all states are subject to and bound by international law. The difference between 'subject to nobody' and 'subject to no other state' is exactly the two-word trap that costs marks in the exam.
slides.22: Equality on paper, and the reality of power. There is a contradiction here that you need to be able to name: formal sovereign equality does not match reality, because states are deeply unequal in economic and political terms, and the rule of one state, one vote does not capture that. At the same time there is a reason why the law keeps growing: ubi interactio, ibi ius — where there is interaction, there is law. As states become more interdependent, more rules appear. A useful exam note: equality is a legal category, not a description of the world.
slides.23: The consent of states — the hinge between the part on sovereignty and the part on sources. Because nobody stands above states, states themselves create, interpret and apply the rules, and the rules bind them because they consented. Consent comes in two forms: express, through treaties; and tacit, in customary law, where it is enough that the state did not object to the emerging rule. The persistent objector doctrine grows out of that second form, and is developed in the later lectures on sources.
slides.24: Article 38 of the Statute of the International Court of Justice. The provision is split in two, and the split is what matters. Paragraphs a, b and c belong together and are the formal sources: international conventions, international custom, and general principles of law. Paragraph d stands apart, labelled subsidiary means, or material sources: judicial decisions and the teachings of publicists are not sources but aids in determining what the rules are. This distinction is the single most common trap in the chapter. Note also that the literal text still carries the period phrase 'civilized nations', which is no longer used but remains in the Statute.
slides.25: Five sources — and which of them are not in Article 38. Treaties, custom and general principles of law are in Article 38. Decisions of international organizations, typically binding Security Council resolutions, and unilateral acts are not in Article 38 — and yet they function as sources. The explanation is historical: the provision dates from 1920 and the catalogue has not been revised since, while practice has moved on. That is itself a usable argument in an essay answer.
slides.26: A decision of an international organization, worked through on a real text: Security Council Resolution 1373 of 2001, adopted three weeks after the eleventh of September. It is introduced by the formula 'Acting under Chapter VII of the Charter' and continues with 'Decides that all States shall' — not 'recommends'. Those words are what turn the resolution into a binding decision for every state, rather than a political declaration. It also imposes general obligations for the future, such as preventing and criminalizing the financing of terrorism, which is why it is described as quasi-legislative action by the Council.
slides.27: Soft law: non-binding resolutions of international organizations, and political declarations. The example used is the Universal Declaration of Human Rights of 1948. The key point is this: the Declaration was not adopted as a binding instrument, and yet it became the starting point of later binding treaties, and part of its content has hardened into custom. Soft law is therefore not weak law. It is non-law that shapes what will become law.
slides.28: The hierarchy of sources, drawn as a temple — and the drawing carries the whole argument, so build it in your head. Five pillars stand side by side at the same height: treaties, custom, unilateral acts, general principles of law, and binding decisions of international organizations. Because they stand at the same height, there is no hierarchy among them. Resting on top of them is the pediment: ius cogens, the peremptory norms that no source may contradict. Below the pillars runs a band of soft law, separated from them by a line called the normative threshold — the line under which something is no longer law. So the hierarchy separates only three levels: peremptory norms, ordinary sources, and soft law.
slides.29: Is international law law? And is it effective? Two questions, answered in two columns. The first column says no, and no: John Austin held that without a central legislature, without compulsory jurisdiction and without a body monopolising force, there is no law — and that collective security is ineffective. The second column says yes, and yes most of the time: reciprocity generates a compliance pull, there is a basic consensus on the validity of the international legal order, and compliance usually pays. What comes now is the elaboration of that second column — how the system is enforced, and what motivates compliance.
slides.30: Enforcement through self-help: countermeasures and retorsion. Because there is no central executive, and judicial settlement remains uncommon, enforcement runs through self-help — and here are two things students routinely confuse. A countermeasure is conduct that would in principle be unlawful, but is not, because its addressee itself previously breached international law; its limits are proportionality and ius cogens. A retaliatory measure, retorsion, is conduct that is lawful but unfriendly — breaking off diplomatic relations, discontinuing economic aid. The first question to ask in the exam: would this conduct be unlawful if no prior breach had occurred?
slides.31: Retorsion in practice. Hangzhou, the fourth of September 2016: President Obama walks down the aircraft's own stairs, and the lecture marks the spot with an arrow and the words 'no red carpet' — the missing carpet at the G20 arrival. Not rolling out a carpet breaches no obligation; it is a demonstrative unfriendly gesture, and therefore a textbook act of retorsion. It puts a face on the distinction just drawn: retorsion is recognised by the fact that no rule is broken at all.
slides.32: Why states comply: the international costs, sorted by where the pressure comes from. Bilaterally, the injured state can reach for countermeasures, retorsion and individual self-defence — all reactions by a single state. Multilaterally the costs rise: exclusion from international organizations, loss of goodwill and reputation, losing disputes before international courts, collective self-defence, Security Council sanctions or authorization of force, non-recognition of territorial gains and of treaties obtained by force, and finally international criminal responsibility. That last item matters because of its addressee: it is not the state that is punished, but the individual who decided.
slides.33: Why states comply: the domestic costs. The last part turns the view inward. Breaking the law does not pay, because it damages the government at home: it hands an advantage to the political opposition, meets resistance from organized interest groups, draws criticism from the media and from non-governmental organizations, and burdens the foreign policy bureaucracy. Together with the international costs, this is the answer to Austin — the system is not enforced by a police force, it is enforced by costs, external and internal alike.
